property_summary: For any oracle version returned by the product, C.currentVersion() must return the oracle's currentVersion with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition (i.e. C applies transform to oracle().currentVersion()); the mutant that returns oracle().currentVersion() directly will sometimes return a different price (untransformed) and thus violate this rule for some oracle prices.

For any oracle version, C.currentVersion() must return the oracle's currentVersion with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition; the mutant that returns oracle().currentVersion() directly will sometimes return a different price (untransformed) and thus break this invariant for some oracle prices.

For every oracle state, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle's currentVersion with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition; the mutant that returns oracle().currentVersion() directly will sometimes return an untransformed price and thus differ (the rule: returned price equals payoffDefinition.transform(oracle.currentVersion().price)).

For any oracle version returned by the product's oracle, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle's currentVersion but with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition; the mutant that forwards oracle().currentVersion() directly will sometimes return an untransformed price, violating equality of the returned price to payoffDefinition.transform(oracle.currentVersion().price).

For every oracle state, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle's currentVersion but with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition; the mutant that forwards oracle().currentVersion() directly will sometimes return an untransformed price, so comparing the price field of C.currentVersion() with oracle().currentVersion() after applying payoffDefinition.transform should hold for the reference and fail for the mutant.

For any state, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle's current version with its price left unchanged (i.e., equal to oracle().currentVersion().price); the mutant sets the returned price to zero breaking this invariant for inputs where oracle().currentVersion().price != 0.

For every input oracle, C.currentVersion() returns an OracleVersion whose price equals oracle().currentVersion().price; the mutant that zeroes the price violates this when the oracle's current price is non-zero.

For any oracle contract, C.currentVersion() returns the same price as oracle().currentVersion().price; the mutant that overwrites the returned price to Fixed18.ZERO will violate this when the oracle's current price is non-zero.

For any oracle whose currentVersion().price is non-zero, C.currentVersion() must return an OracleVersion with the same non-zero price; the mutant that forces the returned price to Fixed18.ZERO breaks this rule for any oracle reporting a non-zero price.

For any deployed oracle contract, C.currentVersion() returns an OracleVersion whose price equals oracle().currentVersion().price; the mutant that overwrites the returned price to Fixed18.ZERO will violate this when the oracle reports a non-zero price.

For any oracle version id, C.atVersion(id) returns the oracle version with price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition.transform (i.e. returned.price == transform(original).price); the mutant returns the untransformed original price for some ids, violating this rule.

For every oracle version id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the transformed price produced by C._transform(original), but the mutant may return the original untransformed price for some ids (i.e. returned.price != transformed.price).

For any oracle version id, calling atVersion(id) on the correct contract returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the transformed price (i.e. _transform(oracle().atVersion(id)).price), while the mutant may return the untransformed original price for some ids.

For every oracle version id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the transformed price (i.e. equal to _transform(original).price); the mutant returns the original untransformed price for some ids, violating this rule.

For any oracle version id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the product of applying payoffDefinition.transform to the oracle's original price (i.e., returned.price == _transform(original).price); the mutant sometimes returns the original untransformed price, violating this property.

For any deployed product contract C, its maintenance() getter always returns the per-product stored maintenance value (not the controller's global minCollateral); the mutant returning controller().minCollateral() will differ for some controller and product states.

For any product C, maintenance() returns the product-specific stored maintenance value; the mutant that returns controller().minCollateral() can differ when the controller's minCollateral is not equal to the product's stored maintenance.

For every product and account, C.maintenance(account) always returns the product's stored per-product maintenance value; the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() instead, so when controller.minCollateral() != product.maintenance() the mutant's maintenance() differs and the property is violated.

For any product C and any account address, the correct contract's maintenance(account) always returns the product's stored per-product maintenance value; the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() instead, so when controller.minCollateral() != product.maintenance() the mutant will return a different value and violate this rule.

For any account address, the reference contract's maintenance(account) always returns the product-specific stored maintenance value (the per-product maintenance), whereas the mutant returns controller().minCollateral(), so there exists an account (and controller configuration) where those two values differ and the mutant breaks the rule.

For every stored _positionFee value, C.positionFee() returns exactly that stored value (identity); the mutant multiplies the stored value by 2, so for some stored values the returned value differs and thus violates the identity property.
For any stored position fee value, the contract's public positionFee() must return exactly that stored value; the mutant doubles the returned value for some inputs, violating this identity.
